plot: Odo and Mothwick follow the true story of Bluff Creek, California (1958): bulldozer driver Jerry Crew finds 16-inch footprints, a plaster cast hits the front page and the name Bigfoot is born, then the 1967 Patterson-Gimlin film appears; the twist is Ray Wallace's family revealing carved wooden feet in 2002, though a crew member disputes it and the film stays unexplained — and a 'tree' steps behind Odo.

beats.say: Look at these! Footprints all around my bulldozer! Huge ones!
A true story. Bluff Creek, northern California, August nineteen fifty-eight.
Sixteen inches long, sunk deep in the mud. So who made them?
New episode every day — subscribe so you don't miss what happens next.
A black noon, a red moon... and now giant footprints.
They come out of the mud, Odo. Straight into the trees.
Jerry Crew drove a bulldozer, cutting a logging road through the forest.
His crew worked for a road contractor named Ray Wallace.
Somebody's pulling a prank on us. It has to be.
But other men said they had seen tracks like these before.
And that oil drum? Four hundred fifty pounds. Something moved it.
The men had a name for whatever was walking there at night.
Bigfoot. That's what we call him. Bigfoot.
They named it... before anyone had even seen it?
When Jerry found more prints, he made a plaster cast of one.
Sixteen inches. My own boot looks tiny next to it.
He took it to Andrew Genzoli, a reporter at the Humboldt Times.
Hold it up, Jerry. Right there. This one's for the front page.
The story spread fast. And the name Bigfoot spread with it.
October sixth, nineteen fifty-eight. Bigfoot was in the paper. Soon, everywhere.
The New York Times came calling. Now the whole country wanted answers.
Nine years later, two men rode up Bluff Creek with a camera.
Bob, look! Across the creek! Get the camera running!
On October twentieth, Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin filmed something walking.
The film runs just under a minute. It is still studied today.
It's turning its head... it's looking straight at them.
Many experts think the film is a hoax. Others still argue.
If those tracks were real, Odo, something huge still walks here.
Then, in two thousand two, Ray Wallace died. Remember that name?
His family shared a secret. Big wooden feet, carved by hand.
Dad made those tracks. Bigfoot started as a joke.
The boss made the footprints? All of them?
His family said relatives used the feet to stamp prank tracks.
But Ed Schillinger, who worked on that road job, strongly disagreed.
Those tracks weren't made with wooden feet. I was there.
And wooden feet cannot explain what walked across that film.
Scientists point out that no bones or body have ever been found.
Many sightings, they say, are bears standing up in poor light.
And still, every year, people come to Bluff Creek to look.
So was it a joke? Or something hiding behind a joke?
The cast, the newspaper, the film. All of them are real.
What made them is still an open question.
Odo. Behind you. That tree just took a step.
Next time, the lantern leads us somewhere new. Don't miss it.
What do you think happens in the next part? Tell me in the comments.

A true story from Bluff Creek, California: in 1958 bulldozer driver Jerry Crew found 16-inch footprints in the mud, and a newspaper gave the world the word Bigfoot. Then came a film in 1967 — and in 2002, a family secret.
